questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: The trace and determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix are known to be \(-2\) and \(-35\) respectively. Its eigenvalues are
questions.explanation:
Given that for a \(2 \times 2\) real square matrix \(A_{2 \times 2}\), its trace and determinant are: \[\text{Trace}(A) = -2, \qquad |A| = -35\] Let \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) be the two eigenvalues of matrix \(A\).
  1. The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of the matrix: \[\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \text{Trace}(A) = -2 \implies \lambda_2 = -2 - \lambda_1 \qquad \text{--- (1)}\]
  2. The product of the eigenvalues equals the determinant of the matrix: \[\lambda_1 \lambda_2 = |A| = -35 \qquad \text{--- (2)}\]
\[\lambda_1 (-2 - \lambda_1) = -35\] \[-2\lambda_1 - \lambda_1^2 = -35\] \[\lambda_1^2 + 2\lambda_1 - 35 = 0\] \[\lambda_1^2 + 7\lambda_1 - 5\lambda_1 - 35 = 0\] \[\lambda_1(\lambda_1 + 7) - 5(\lambda_1 + 7) = 0\] \[(\lambda_1 + 7)(\lambda_1 - 5) = 0\] \[\lambda_1 = -7 \quad \text{or} \quad \lambda_1 = 5\] Thus, the two eigenvalues of the matrix are \(-7\) and \(5\). \[\boxed{\text{(C) -7 and 5}}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: If \(f(x, y)\) is continuous function defined over \((x, y) \in [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\). Given two constraints, \(x > y^2\) and \(y > x^2\), the volume under \(f(x, y)\) is
questions.explanation:
Given that \(f(x, y)\) is a continuous function defined over the domain: \[(x, y) \in [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\] The region of integration is bounded by two constraints:
  • \(x > y^2 \implies x = y^2\) is a rightward-opening parabola.
  • \(y > x^2 \implies y = x^2\) is an upward-opening parabola (which can be rewritten as \(x = \sqrt{y}\) for the upper boundary curve in the first quadrant).
Let us find the intersection points of these two curves: \[y = (y^2)^2 \implies y = y^4\] \[y(y^3 - 1) = 0 \implies y = 0 \text{ or } y = 1\] Substituting these values back to find \(x\):
  • If \(y = 0 \implies x = 0^2 = 0\). The first intersection point is \((0, 0)\).
  • If \(y = 1 \implies x = 1^2 = 1\). The second intersection point is \((1, 1)\).
To find the volume under \(f(x, y)\), we set up a double integral over this bounded region. Stripping the region horizontally using a horizontal line segment (parallel to the \(x\)-axis):
  • Inner limits (\(x\)-limits): The left end of the strip rests on the curve \(x = y^2\), and the right end of the strip touches the curve \(x = \sqrt{y}\). Therefore, the limits for \(x\) are: \[x = y^2 \quad \text{to} \quad x = \sqrt{y}\]
  • Outer limits (\(y\)-limits): The horizontal strip sweeps the entire bounded region vertically from the bottom intersection point to the top intersection point. Therefore, the limits for \(y\) are: \[y = 0 \quad \text{to} \quad y = 1\]
Expressing this as a double integral: \[\text{Volume} = \int_{y=0}^{y=1} \int_{x=y^2}^{x=\sqrt{y}} f(x, y) \,dx \,dy\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) } \int_{y=0}^{y=1} \int_{x=y^2}^{x=\sqrt{y}} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: \(\vec{F}(x,y) = (x^2 + xy)\hat{a}_x + (y^2 + xy)\hat{a}_y\). Its line integral over the straight line from \((x,y) = (0,2)\) to \((x,y) = (2,0)\) evaluates to
questions.explanation:
Given, \[\vec{F}(x,y)=(x^2+xy)\hat{a}_x+(y^2+xy)\hat{a}_y\] The straight line joining \((0,2)\) and \((2,0)\) is \[x+y=2\] Hence, \[y=2-x\] and \[dy=-dx\] The line integral is \[\int_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}
=
\int_C \left[(x^2+xy)\,dx+(y^2+xy)\,dy\right]\] Substituting \(y=2-x\), \[x^2+x(2-x)=2x\] Also, \[y^2+xy=(2-x)^2+x(2-x)=4-2x\] Therefore, \[\int_0^2 \left[2x\,dx+(4-2x)(-dx)\right]\] \[=
\int_0^2 (4x-4)\,dx\] \[=
\left[2x^2-4x\right]_0^2\] \[=
8-8=0\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) } 0}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: Assume for simplicity that \(N\) people, all born in April (a month of 30 days) are collected in a room, consider the event of at least two people in the room being born on the same date of the month even if in different years e.g. 1980 and 1985. What is the smallest \(N\) so that the probability of this exceeds \(0.5\) is?
questions.explanation:
Let the event ``at least two people have the same birth date'' be \(E\). We first calculate the complement event: \[E^{c}=\text{all birthdays are different}\] Since April has \(30\) days, \[P(E^{c})=\frac{30}{30}\times\frac{29}{30}\times\frac{28}{30}\times \cdots \times \frac{30-N+1}{30}\] We need \[P(E)>0.5\] That is, \[1-P(E^{c})>0.5\] \[P(E^{c})<0.5\] Checking the options: For \(N=7\), \[P(E^{c})=\frac{30\times29\times28\times27\times26\times25\times24}{30^7}
\approx 0.459\] Hence, \[P(E)=1-0.459=0.541>0.5\] Now for \(N=6\), \[P(E^{c})\approx 0.593\] \[P(E)\approx 0.407<0.5\] Therefore, the smallest value of \(N\) is \[7\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }7}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: Let \(x^2 - 117 = 0\). The iterative steps for the solution using Newton-Raphson's method is given by
questions.explanation:
We are given the quadratic root equation \(x^2 - 117 = 0\). Let \(f(x) = x^2 - 117\). Differentiating with respect to \(x\) gives: \[f'(x) = 2x\] Substitute these expressions into the general Newton-Raphson formula: \[x_{k+1} = x_k - \dfrac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}\] \[x_{k+1} = x_k - \dfrac{x_k^2 - 117}{2x_k}\] Find a common denominator to combine the terms: \[\begin{aligned} x_{k+1} &= \dfrac{2x_k^2 - \left(x_k^2 - 117\right)}{2x_k} \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{x_k^2 + 117}{2x_k} \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left( \dfrac{x_k^2}{x_k} + \dfrac{117}{x_k} \right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left( x_k + \dfrac{117}{x_k} \right) \end{aligned}\] This derived relation matches Option A. \[\boxed{\text{A. } x_{k+1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_k + \dfrac{117}{x_k}\right)}\]
Key points
  • Babylonian Method Link: Finding the square root of a number \(A\) using the Newton-Raphson method (\(\sqrt{A}\)) simplifies directly to the classic Babylonian recursive averaging algorithm: \[x_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_k + \frac{A}{x_k}\right)\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: In the figure shown, all elements used are ideal. For time \(t < 0\), \(S_1\) remained closed and \(S_2\) open. At \(t = 0\), \(S_1\) is opened and \(S_2\) is closed. If the voltage \(V_{\text{c2}}\) across the capacitor \(C_2\) at \(t = 0\) is zero, the voltage across the capacitor combination at \(t = 0^{+}\) will be
questions.explanation:
For \(t<0\) \(S_1\) is closed and \(S_2\) is open. Hence, capacitor \(C_1\) is connected across the \(3~\text{V}\) source and reaches steady state. \[\Rightarrow V_{C_1}(0^-)=3~\text{V},\quad V_{C_2}(0^-)=0~\text{V}\] Since capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously, \[V_{C_1}(0^+)=3~\text{V} \quad \text{and} \quad V_{C_2}(0^+)=0~\text{V}\] At \(t=0\)
Method 1
Since there is no resistor in the circuit, total charge is conserved. Initial charge stored in \(C_1\) is \[Q_{\text{initial}} = C_1V_{C_1}(0^-) = 1\times3 = 3~\text{C}\] Initial charge on \(C_2\) is 0 Hence, \[Q_{\text{total}} = 3~\text{C}\] After connection, both capacitors attain the same voltage \(V\). Therefore, \[Q_{\text{total}} = (C_1+C_2)V \ \Rightarrow \ 3 = (1+2)V\] \[V=1~\text{V}\] Thus, the voltage across the capacitor combination at \(t=0^+\) is 1V
Method 2
When two capacitors having initial voltages \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) are connected, then by charge distribution, \[V_f = \frac{C_1V_1+C_2V_2} {C_1+C_2} \qquad \text{(where \(V_f\) is the final voltage across cap. after charge sharing)}\] Substituting, \[V_f = \frac{(1)(3)+(2)(0)} {1+2}\] \[V_f = 1~\text{V}\] Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }1~\text{V}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: The equivalent capacitance of the input loop of the circuit shown below is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
For a capacitor, \[Q=CV, \qquad \text{For constant voltage; }\ Q \propto C\] and \[i=\frac{dQ}{dt} \Rightarrow C \propto i\] The current through middle 100\(\mu\)F is, \[i_s = i_1+49i_1 = 50i_1\] Since capacitance is proportional to current for constant voltage, \[\frac{C_{eq}}{100\mu F} = \frac{i_1}{50i_1}\] \[C_{eq} = \frac{100}{50}\mu F\] \[C_{eq} = 2\mu F\]
Method 2
Let \[R=1~k\Omega, \qquad C=100~\mu F\] By KVL; \[V_{in} = 2Ri_1 + \frac{50i_1}{j\omega C}\] Representing the entire network by an equivalent capacitance \(C_{eq}\), \[V_{in} = 2Ri_1 + \frac{i_1}{j\omega C_{eq}}\] Comparing the capacitive terms, \[\frac{i_1}{j\omega C_{eq}} = \frac{50i_1}{j\omega C}\] \[C_{eq} = \frac{C}{50}\] \[C_{eq} = \frac{100}{50}\mu F = 2\mu F\] Hence, \[\boxed{C_{eq}=2~\mu F}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }2~\mu F}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A cascade of \(3\) Linear Time Invariant systems is causal and unstable. From this, we conclude that
options: Each system in the cascade is individually causal and unstable
At least one system is unstable and at least one system is causal
At least one system is causal and all systems are unstable
The majority are unstable and the majority are causal
questions.explanation:
A cascade of three LTI systems is given to be causal and unstable. Causality:
A cascade is causal only if each individual system is causal. If even one system is non-causal, the overall cascade becomes non-causal. Hence, all three systems must be causal. Stability:
For a cascade of LTI systems to be BIBO stable, every individual system must be stable. Since the overall cascade is unstable, at least one of the systems must be unstable. Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{At least one system is unstable and at least one system is causal.}}\] Checking the options:
  • A. False: Every system need not be unstable.
  • B. True: At least one system is unstable, and since all systems are causal, at least one system is certainly causal.
  • C. False: It is not necessary that all systems are unstable.
  • D. False: No conclusion can be made about the majority being unstable.
\[\boxed{\text{(b) At least one system is unstable and at least one system is causal}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A Linear Time Invariant system with an impulse response \(h(t)\) produces output \(y(t)\) when the input \(x(t)\) is applied. When the input \(x(t-\tau)\) is applied to a system with impulse response \(h(t-\tau)\), the output will be
questions.explanation:
For the original LTI system, \[y(t)=x(t)*h(t).\] Now the modified input and impulse response are \[x_{1}(t)=x(t-\tau),\qquad
h_{1}(t)=h(t-\tau).\] The new output is \[\begin{aligned}
y_{1}(t)
&=x_{1}(t)*h_{1}(t) \\
&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
x(\lambda-\tau)\,
h(t-\tau-\lambda)\,d\lambda.
\end{aligned}\] Let \[u=\lambda-\tau
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
d\lambda=du.\] Then, \[\begin{aligned}
y_{1}(t)
&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
x(u)\,
h(t-2\tau-u)\,du \\
&=y(t-2\tau).
\end{aligned}\] Thus, delaying both the input and the impulse response by \(\tau\) delays the output by \(2\tau\). \[\boxed{\text{(d) }y(t-2\tau)}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
options: \(x(t)\) has finite energy because only finitely many coefficients are non-zero
\(x(t)\) has zero average value because it is periodic
The imaginary part of \(x(t)\) is constant
The real part of \(x(t)\) is even
questions.explanation:
Given Fourier series coefficients, \[a_{-2}=2-j,\quad a_{-1}=0.5+j0.2,\quad a_{0}=j2,\quad a_{1}=0.5-j0.2,\quad a_{2}=2+j,\quad a_k=0,\; |k|>2.\] Since only finitely many Fourier series coefficients are non-zero, the signal is still periodic. Therefore, \[\text{Energy of }x(t)=\infty,\] so Option A is incorrect. The average (DC) value is \[a_{0}=\frac{1}{T_{0}}\int_{-T_{0}/2}^{T_{0}/2}x(t)\,dt=j2\neq0,\] hence Option B is also incorrect. The coefficients satisfy \[a_k=a_{-k}^{*},\qquad k\neq0.\] Thus, all non-DC harmonics combine to produce a purely real signal. The only imaginary contribution comes from \[a_{0}=j2,\] which is a constant (DC) term. Hence, \[x(t)=x_r(t)+j2,\] where \(x_r(t)\) is real. Therefore, \[\Im\{x(t)\}=2,\] which is constant. \[\boxed{\text{(c) The imaginary part of }x(t)\text{ is constant}}\]
Key points
  • A periodic signal has infinite energy but finite average power.
  • The DC Fourier coefficient \(a_{0}\) equals the average value of the signal.
  • If \(a_k=a_{-k}^{*}\) for \(k\neq0\), the non-DC harmonics contribute only to the real part of the signal.
  • A purely imaginary \(a_{0}\) contributes only a constant imaginary component.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not conclude finite energy from finitely many Fourier coefficients.
  • Do not assume the average value is zero for every periodic signal.
  • Do not infer symmetry of the real part without verifying all Fourier coefficients, including the DC term.

questions.ref: Z Transform, DTFS and DTFT Q1
questions.question: The \(z\)-transform of a signal \(x[n]\) is given by \[4z^{-3}+3z^{-1}+2-6z^2+2z^3.\] It is applied to a system, with a transfer function \[H(z)=3z^{-1}-2.\] Let the output be \(y(n)\). Which of the following is true?
options: \(y(n)\) is non causal with finite support.
questions.explanation:
Given, \[X(z)=4z^{-3}+3z^{-1}+2-6z^2+2z^3,\] and \[H(z)=3z^{-1}-2.\] The output is \[Y(z)=H(z)X(z).\] Expanding, \[\begin{aligned}
Y(z)
&=(3z^{-1}-2)(4z^{-3}+3z^{-1}+2-6z^2+2z^3)\\
&=-4z^3+18z^2-18z+12z^{-4}+9z^{-2}-4-8z^{-3}.
\end{aligned}\] Since \[Y(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}y[n]z^{-n},\] positive powers of \(z\) correspond to samples with \(n<0\). As \(Y(z)\) contains positive powers \(z,\;z^2,\;z^3\), the sequence \(y[n]\) is non-causal. Also, \(Y(z)\) contains only finitely many powers of \(z\), so \(y[n]\) has finite support. Hence, the output is a non-causal finite-duration sequence. \[\boxed{\text{(a) }y[n]\text{ is non-causal with finite support.}}\]

questions.question: The following circuit has a source voltage \(V_{\text{S}}\) as shown in the graph. The current through the circuit is also shown. The element connected between \(\textbf{a}\) and \(\textbf{b}\) could be
questions.explanation:
For different intervals of time, For \(0<t<100~\text{ms},\) \[V_s=0 \ \Rightarrow \ i=0\] For \(100<t<200~\text{ms},\) \[V_s=10~\text{V}\] The current through the resistor is \[i
=
\frac{10}{10~\text{k}\Omega}
=
1~\text{mA}\] Thus, the element conducts during the positive voltage. For \(200<t<300~\text{ms},\) \[V_s=-10~\text{V}\] From the given current waveform, a negative current flows initially and then decays to zero. This is the reverse recovery current exhibited by a diode when it is suddenly reverse biased. After the reverse recovery time, the diode becomes reverse biased and blocks the current. For \(300<t<400~\text{ms},\) \[V_s=0 \ \Rightarrow \ i=0\] Therefore, the element connected between terminals \(a\) and \(b\) is a diode with anode at \(a\) and cathode at \(b\). Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A}}\]

questions.question: The nature of feedback in the op-amp circuit shown is
questions.explanation:
Output Sampling Analysis:
  • The feedback network is connected directly across the output node \(V_{\text{out}}\).
  • Sampling the output voltage directly corresponds to voltage sampling (node sampling).
Input Mixing Analysis:
  • The feedback signal is fed back to the inverting terminal while input \(V_{\text{in}}\) is applied to the non-inverting terminal.
  • Mixing at different nodes (series connection) corresponds to series (voltage) mixing.
Hence, it is a voltage-series or voltage-voltage feedback topology. \[\boxed{\text{(B) voltage-voltage feedback}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The following circuit has \(R = 10\text{ k}\Omega\), \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F}\). The input voltage is a sinusoid at \(50\text{Hz}\) with an rms value of \(10\text{V}\). Under ideal conditions, the current \(i_S\) from the source is
questions.explanation: The current entering the non-inverting terminal from the source is: \[i_s = \frac{V_s - V_o}{R}\] By the virtual short concept, \(V_- = V_+ = V_s\). Voltage divider at the inverting terminal yields: \[V_s = \frac{\frac{1}{j\omega C}}{R + \frac{1}{j\omega C}} V_o = \frac{V_o}{1 + j\omega CR}\] \[\implies V_o = V_s(1 + j\omega CR)\] Substituting \(V_o\) into the source current equation: \[i_s = \frac{V_s - V_s(1 + j\omega CR)}{R} = -j\omega C V_s\] Given \(V_s = 10\,\text{V}\), \(f = 50\,\text{Hz}\), \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F}\): \[i_s = -j(2\pi \times 50 \times 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 10)\] \[i_s = -j10\pi\,\text{mA} = 10\pi\text{ mA} \angle -90^\circ\] \[\boxed{(D) \ \ 10\pi\text{ mA} \  \text{lagging by} \ 90^\circ}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An ideal opamp circuit and its input waveform are shown in the figures. The output waveform of this circuit will be
questions.explanation:
This is an inverting Schmitt trigger circuit. The upper and lower threshold voltages are calculated as: \[V_{\text{UTP}} = +V_{\text{sat}} \times \frac{1}{2 + 1} = 6 \times \frac{1}{3} = 2\,\text{V}\] \[V_{\text{LTP}} = -V_{\text{sat}} \times \frac{1}{1 + 2} = -3 \times \frac{1}{3} = -1\,\text{V}\] Waveform Generation:
  • Initially, \(V_o = +6\,\text{V}\). The output remains at \(+6\,\text{V}\) until \(V_i\) rises above \(V_{\text{UTP}} = 2\,\text{V}\) at time \(t_2\).
  • At \(t = t_2\), \(V_o\) switches to \(-3\,\text{V}\) and stays there until \(V_i\) falls below \(V_{\text{LTP}} = -1\,\text{V}\) at time \(t_4\).
  • At \(t = t_4\), \(V_o\) switches back to \(+6\,\text{V}\).
\[\boxed{\text{(D)}}\]
Key points
Asymmetric Saturation: Thresholds depend on saturation levels: \(V_{\text{UTP}} = \dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} V_{\text{sat}}^{+}\) and \(V_{\text{LTP}} = \dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} V_{\text{sat}}^{-}\).

questions.question: The complete set of only those Logic Gates designated as Universal Gates is
questions.explanation:
Using either NOR or NAND gate, all possible logic gates can be implemented. Hence, NOR and NAND are designated as universal logic gates.
Key points
  • NAND gate: Can implement NOT, AND, OR, NOR, XNOR, XOR.
  • NOR gate: Can implement NOT, OR, AND, NAND, XOR, XNOR.
  • XOR and XNOR are special purpose gates, not universal.
Hence, the correct option is (C). (C) NOR and NAND Gates

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The unit-step response of a unity feedback system with open loop transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}\) is shown in the figure. The value of \(K\) is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
From the given response curve, the steady-state final value of the system response is: \(C_{ss} = 0.75\) Since the input is a unit-step input (\(R = 1\)), the steady-state error (\(e_{ss}\)) is: \[e_{ss} = 1 - C_{ss} = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25\] \[e_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{s R(s)}{1 + G(s)H(s)}\] Substituting \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\) and \(G(s) = \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}\): \[e_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{s \cdot \dfrac{1}{s}}{1 + \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}} = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{K}{2}}\] Equating this to the observed value: \[\frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{K}{2}} = 0.25 \implies K = 6\]
Method 2
The closed-loop transfer function \(T(s)\) is: \[T(s) = \frac{G(s)}{1 + G(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}}{1 + \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}}\] \[T(s) = \frac{K}{s^2 + 3s + (2 + K)}\] Using the final value theorem, the steady-state value for a unit-step input is: \[C_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot C(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \left[ T(s) \cdot \frac{1}{s} \right]\] \[C_{ss} = T(0) = \frac{K}{2 + K}\] From the given curve, \(C_{ss} = 0.75 = \dfrac{3}{4}\): \[\frac{K}{2 + K} = \frac{3}{4}\] \[4K = 6 + 3K \implies K = 6\]
\[\boxed{(D) \ \ 6}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
The first two rows of Routh's tabulation of a third order equation are as follows.
\(s^3\)22
\(s^2\)44
This means there are
options: two roots at \(s = \pm j\) and one root in right half s-plane
two roots at \(s = \pm j2\) and one root in left half s-plane
two roots at \(s = \pm j2\) and one root in right half s-plane
two roots at \(s = \pm j\) and one root in left half s-plane
questions.explanation:
RH Array:
\[\begin{array}{r|cc} s^3 & 2 & 2 \\ s^2 & 4 & 4 \\ s^1 & 0(8) \\ s^0 & 4 \end{array}\] Auxiliary Equation: \(A(s) = 4s^2 + 4 = 0\) Differentiating with respect to \(s\): \[\frac{d}{ds}A(s) = \frac{d}{ds}(4s^2 + 4) = 8s + 0\] Roots of the auxiliary equation: \[4s^2 + 4 = 0 \implies s = \pm j1\] Therefore, there are two roots at \(s = \pm j\). Since there is no sign change in the first column of the Routh array, the remaining one root will lie in the left half of the \(s\)-plane. \[\boxed{\text{(D) two roots at $s = \pm j$ and one root in left half s-plane}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The polar plot of an open loop stable system is shown below. The closed loop system is
options: unstable with one pole on the RH s-plane
unstable with two poles on the RH s-plane
questions.explanation:
From the polar plot, the locus crosses the negative real axis at \((-1.42, j0)\). Now if we draw the complete nyquist plot, it would be: The plot encircles the critical point \((-1,j0)\) once in the clockwise direction. Assuming the Nyquist Contour is in clock wise direction, hence, \(N=-2\) It is given that the open-loop system is stable. Hence, \(P=0\) By Nyquist criterion, \[N=P-Z\] \[-2=0-Z\] \[Z=2\] Therefore, the closed-loop system has two poles in the right half plane and is unstable. \[\boxed{\text{(D) Unstable with two poles on the RH s-plane}}\]
Key points
  • Nyquist criterion: \[N=P-Z\]
    • \(N\) = encirclements of \((-1,j0)\) by \(G(s)\)
    • \(P\) = number of right half plane poles of \(G(s)\)
    • \(Z\) = number of right half plane zeros of \(1+G(s)\)
  • If \(Z>0\), the closed-loop system is unstable.

The star-delta transformer shown above is excited on the star side with a balanced, \(4\)-wire, \(3\)-phase, sinusoidal voltage supply of rated magnitude. The transformer is under no load condition.

With both S1 and S2 open, the core flux waveform will be
questions.explanation: With both \(S_{1}\) and \(S_{2}\) open, the neutral paths are open. Hence, the third-harmonic magnetizing current cannot flow. For a transformer core, if the third-harmonic component of magnetizing current is suppressed, the core flux becomes distorted and contains a third-harmonic component. This distortion makes the flux waveform flat-topped. \[\therefore \text{Core flux waveform is flat-topped with third harmonic.}\] \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]

Statement for Linked Questions (Q2.09.2 and Q2.09.3):
The star-delta transformer shown above is excited on the star side with a balanced, \(4\)-wire, \(3\)-phase, sinusoidal voltage supply of rated magnitude. The transformer is under no load condition.

With S2 closed and S1 open, the current waveform in the delta winding will be
questions.explanation:
When \(S_{2}\) is closed and no load is connected, the secondary winding forms a closed delta. Since no external load is connected, the fundamental component of secondary current is zero. \[I_{2,\text{fundamental}}=0\] However, third-harmonic currents can circulate in the closed delta path. \[I_{2}=I_{3}+I_{9}+I_{15}+\cdots\] Hence, the secondary current contains only third-harmonic components. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • A closed delta provides a path for third-harmonic circulating currents.
  • With no external load, the fundamental component of secondary current is zero.
  • Triplen harmonics can circulate within the closed delta loop.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume load current flows when no load is connected.
  • Do not ignore the closed delta path for third-harmonic currents.

questions.question: A \(3\)-phase squirrel cage induction motor supplied from a balanced \(3\)-phase source drives a mechanical load. The torque-speed characteristics of the motor (solid curve) and of the load (dotted curve) are shown. Of the two equilibrium points A and B, which of the following options correctly describe the stability of A and B? [figure unavailable]
options: A is stable B is unstable
A is unstable B is stable
questions.explanation:
For an induction motor, the condition for stable operation is \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}\] where \(T_{e}\) is the electromagnetic torque and \(T_{L}\) is the load torque. The tangents at the operating points are shown in the figure. At point \(A\), \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}>\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] Hence, point \(A\) satisfies the stability criterion and is a stable operating point. At point \(B\), the slope of the load torque characteristic is more negative than that of the motor torque characteristic. Therefore, \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] Hence, point \(B\) does not satisfy the stability criterion and is an unstable operating point. Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Stability of an induction motor operating point is determined by comparing the slopes of motor and load torque characteristics.
  • Stable operation requires \(\dfrac{dT_{e}}{dn}<\dfrac{dT_{L}}{dn}\).
  • At a stable operating point, a small speed disturbance produces a restoring torque.
  • The sign and magnitude of the slopes at the intersection point are more important than the torque values themselves.

questions.question:
Out of the following plant categories
  1. Nuclear
  2. Run-of-river
  3. Pump Storage
  4. Diesel
The base-load power plants are
questions.explanation:
Base-load power plants are generating stations that operate continuously to supply the minimum demand of the power system. Nuclear power plants
  • Have very high capital cost.
  • Have very low running cost.
  • Are most economical when operated continuously.
  • Therefore, they are used as base-load stations.
Run-of-river hydro plants
  • Generate power continuously depending on river flow.
  • Are generally used to meet base-load demand.
Pumped-storage plants
  • Are primarily used for peak-load operation and load balancing.
  • Hence, they are not base-load plants.
Diesel power plants
  • Have high operating cost.
  • Are generally used for standby, emergency and peak-load duties.
  • Hence, they are not base-load plants.
Therefore, the base-load power plants are \[\boxed{\text{(A) (i) Nuclear and (ii) Run-of-river}}\]

For the Y-bus matrix of a 4-bus system given in per unit, the buses having shunt elements are \[Y_{\text{BUS}} = j \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2 & 2.5 & 0\\ 2 & -10 & 2.5 & 4\\ 2.5 & 2.5 & -9 & 4\\ 0 & 4 & 4 & -8 \end{bmatrix}\]
questions.explanation: Given, \[Y_{\text{BUS}} = j \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2 & 2.5 & 0\\ 2 & -10 & 2.5 & 4\\ 2.5 & 2.5 & -9 & 4\\ 0 & 4 & 4 & -8 \end{bmatrix}\] For a bus-admittance matrix, \[Y_{ii} = Y_{i0} + \sum_{k\neq i} Y_{ik}\] where \(Y_{i0}\) represents the shunt admittance connected to bus \(i\). From the matrix, \[Y_{11} = -5j, \quad Y_{12} = 2j, \quad Y_{13} = 2.5j, \quad Y_{14} = 0\] Hence, \[Y_{10} = Y_{11}-Y_{12}-Y_{13}-Y_{14}\] \[= -5j+2j+2.5j+0 = -0.5j\] Similarly, \[Y_{20} = Y_{22}-Y_{21}-Y_{23}-Y_{24}\] \[= -10j+2j+2.5j+4j = -1.5j\] \[Y_{30} = Y_{33}-Y_{31}-Y_{32}-Y_{34}\] \[= -9j+2.5j+2.5j+4j = 0\] \[Y_{40} = Y_{44}-Y_{41}-Y_{42}-Y_{43}\] \[= -8j+0+4j+4j = 0\] Therefore, \[Y_{10}\neq0, \qquad Y_{20}\neq0\] while \[Y_{30}=0, \qquad Y_{40}=0\] Thus, shunt elements are connected at buses 1 and 2. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(C) Buses 1 and 2}}\]

(a) Short Line(1) Ohm Relay
(b) Medium Line(2) Reactance Relay
(c) Long Line(3) Mho Relay
questions.explanation:
The preferred distance relay depends on the transmission-line length and the corresponding operating characteristics. (a) Short transmission line
For short transmission lines, the line impedance is relatively small and the fault resistance effect is significant. An impedance (Ohm) relay provides satisfactory protection. \[(a)\rightarrow(1)\] (b) Medium transmission line
For medium-length transmission lines, a reactance relay is generally preferred because its operation is largely independent of fault resistance. \[(b)\rightarrow(2)\] (c) Long transmission line
For long transmission lines, power swings and load encroachment become important considerations. A mho relay possesses inherent directional characteristics and is therefore widely used. \[(c)\rightarrow(3)\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(C)} \ a\rightarrow1,\ b\rightarrow2,\ c\rightarrow3}\]

questions.question: The figure shows a three-phase delta connected load supplied from a \(400\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\), \(3\)-phase balanced source. The pressure coil (PC) and current coil (CC) of a wattmeter are connected to the load as shown, with the coil polarities suitably selected to ensure a positive deflection. The wattmeter reading will be [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: For a wattmeter, \[W=V_{PC}I_{CC}\cos\phi\] where \[V_{PC}=\text{voltage across pressure coil},\qquad I_{CC}=\text{current through current coil}\] [figure unavailable] From the circuit, the load is delta connected and \[Z_1=Z_2=(100+j0)\,\Omega\] The source voltage is \[V_{Line}=400\,\text{V}\] For a delta load, \[V_{\text{phase}}=V_{Line}\] Thus, branch voltage across \(Z_2\) is \[V_{ac}=400\,\text{V}\] Hence current through branch \(Z_2\) (and through CC) is \[I_{CC}=\frac{400}{100}=4\,\text{A}\] Since \(Z_2\) is resistive, \(I_{CC}\) is in phase with \(V_{ac}\). The pressure coil is connected across \(b-c\), so \[V_{PC}=V_{bc}\] Taking balanced sequence (\(V_{ab}\) as reference) \[V_{ab}=400\angle 0^\circ,\qquad V_{bc}=400\angle -120^\circ,\qquad V_{ac}=400\angle -60^\circ\] Thus, \[I_{CC}=4\angle -60^\circ\] Angle between \(V_{PC}\) and \(I_{CC}\) is \[\phi=(-60^\circ)-(-120^\circ)=60^\circ\] Therefore, \[W=400\times4\times\cos60^\circ=800\,\text{W}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }800 \text{W}}\]

questions.subject: measurements
questions.question: The pressure coil of a dynamometer type wattmeter is
questions.explanation: In a dynamometer type wattmeter, the pressure coil is connected across the supply voltage. To measure true power, \[P=VI\cos\phi\] the pressure coil current must remain nearly in phase with the applied voltage. If the pressure coil were inductive, \[Z_p=R_p+jX_p\] then pressure coil current \(I_p\) would lag the voltage, causing phase error and incorrect wattmeter reading. To reduce this error, a large non-inductive resistance is connected in series with the pressure coil so that \[R_p\gg X_p\] Hence, \[Z_p\approx R_p\] Therefore, pressure coil current becomes nearly in phase with voltage. Thus, the pressure coil behaves as: \[\boxed{\text{Highly resistive}}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{Highly resistive}}\]

options: The amplitudes of the signals are very close but not equal
The signals are sinusoidal with their frequencies very close but not equal
There is a constant but small phase difference between the signals
questions.explanation:
In the X--Y mode of a CRO:
  • one signal is applied to the X-plates
  • the other signal is applied to the Y-plates
If both signals are sinusoidal and have the same frequency, a Lissajous figure is obtained. For: \[x=A\sin\omega t,\qquad y=B\sin(\omega t+\phi)\] the shape depends on the phase difference \(\phi\). \[\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Phase Difference} & \textbf{Pattern} \\ \hline \phi=0^\circ & \text{Straight line} \\ \hline 0^\circ<\phi<90^\circ & \text{Tilted ellipse} \\ \hline \phi=90^\circ & \text{Circle (if amplitudes equal)} \\ \hline 90^\circ<\phi<180^\circ & \text{Ellipse with opposite tilt} \\ \hline \end{array}\] The figure changes: \[\text{ellipse} \rightarrow \text{circle} \rightarrow \text{ellipse}\] with changing orientation, indicating a varying phase difference between two sinusoidal signals of the same frequency. Hence the correct option is: \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }\text{There is a constant but small phase difference between the signals}}\]
